name: Akkub
title: Levite and Temple Gatekeeper After the Exile
summary: Akkub was a Levite and temple gatekeeper (doorkeeper) who served at the temple in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. He belonged to one of the gatekeeping families that returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel, and his descendants continued to guard the gates and storehouses of the temple. Akkub is mentioned repeatedly in Ezra and Nehemiah as a central figure among the gatekeepers, serving at both the temple gates and the storage rooms. He is also listed among the Levites who were present when Ezra read the law aloud to the people and helped the listeners understand its content, although it is debated whether this refers to the same person. Another individual with the same name is mentioned in 1 Chronicles as a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel's line, but this is likely not the same Akkub.

versions.summary: Akkub was one of the temple gatekeepers (doorkeepers) who served at the temple in Jerusalem after returning from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned several times in Ezra and Nehemiah as part of the Levites' service, and his descendants continued to serve as gatekeepers at God's house. The name Akkub is also borne by other individuals in the Bible, including a descendant of David.

footnotes.text: The name Akkub (Hebrew: עַקּוּב, ʿAqqūḇ) is derived from the root ʿ-q-b, which can mean 'to guard', 'to hold back' or 'to follow'. The root is the same as in the name Jacob (Yaʿaqoḇ), often interpreted as 'he who holds the heel' or 'he who follows'. For a gatekeeper, the meaning 'to guard' carries an appropriate connotation.

The gatekeepers (Hebrew: שׁוֹעֲרִים, šôʿărîm) played an important role in temple service. They guarded the entrances, controlled access to the holy areas and protected the temple's supplies. This service was hereditary and belonged to specific Levitical families who had been given this responsibility already from David's time (1 Chron 9:17–26).

The lists of those who returned from exile in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are important historical sources for understanding the reorganization of the Jewish community after the Babylonian exile. The gatekeepers are mentioned here as a distinct service category separate from the priests and other Levites, although they belonged to the tribe of Levi.

In rabbinic tradition, the gatekeepers were counted among the lower temple servants, but their role was still regarded as holy and necessary. The Mishnah (Middot 1:1) describes in detail the gatekeeping system at the temple, including the number of guard posts and their locations.

There are several individuals named Akkub in the Old Testament: a temple gatekeeper (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45; 11:19; 12:25), a Levite who helped with the reading of the Law (Neh 8:7), and a descendant of King David through Zerubbabel's line (1 Chron 3:24). It is debated whether the gatekeeper and the Levite in Nehemiah 8 are the same person.

Archaeological finds from Persian-period Jerusalem, including seal impressions and ostraca, confirm that the temple was rebuilt and that an organized temple service was in place during this period, consistent with the biblical accounts describing the return of the gatekeeping families.
